---
title: "Day 2 — The Grammar of Wrangling"
subtitle: "Week 2 · dplyr's 6 verbs ↔ the pandas method chain; row-wise ops; one obvious way"
---

## Cheat sheet (60 seconds)

| dplyr verb | job | pandas idiom |
|---|---|---|
| `filter(df, cond)` | pick **rows** | `df.query("cond")` or `df[mask]` |
| `select(df, a, b)` | pick **columns** | `df[["a", "b"]]` / `df.filter(items=...)` |
| `arrange(df, desc(x))` | sort rows | `df.sort_values("x", ascending=False)` |
| `mutate(df, z = a + b)` | new/changed **columns** | `df.assign(z=...)` |
| `group_by(g) |> summarise(m = mean(x))` | split → apply → combine | `df.groupby("g")["x"].mean()` |
| `pull(df, x)` | extract a bare vector | `df["x"]` (a Series) |
| `count(df, g)` | tally | `df.value_counts("g")` |
| `distinct(df)` | dedupe rows | `df.drop_duplicates()` |
| `slice_max(df, x, n = 5)` | top-n rows | `df.nlargest(5, "x")` |
| `rename(df, y = x)` | rename columns | `df.rename(columns={"x": "y"})` |
| `across(a:b, mean)` | apply to many cols | `df[["a","b"]].agg("mean")` |
| `rowwise() |> mutate(...)` | row-by-row | `df.apply(..., axis=1)` (last resort!) |

## One grammar, two dialects

dplyr's insight: data wrangling has a small **vocabulary of verbs**, and any
analysis is a sentence — `starwars |> filter(height > 200) |> select(name,
height) |> arrange(desc(height))`. pandas' insight: the DataFrame knows these
moves as **methods**, so the same sentence is a method chain. Neither wants
your `for` loop over rows. **The verb grammar transfers; only the syntax
changes** — which is why we practice side-by-side.

```{webr}
#| label: sentence-r
library(tidyverse)

starwars |>
  filter(species == "Human", height > 185) |>
  select(name, height, mass) |>
  arrange(desc(mass)) |>
  mutate(bmi = mass / (height / 100)^2)
```

```{pyodide}
#| label: sentence-py
import pandas as pd
starwars = pd.DataFrame({
  "name":    ["Djarin", "Kylo", "Hux", "Finn"],
  "species": ["Human", "Human", "Human", "Human"],
  "height":  [180 + 8, 189, 170, 178],
  "mass":    [80 + 20, 89, 80, 73]})

(starwars
  .query("species == 'Human' and height > 185")
  [["name", "height", "mass"]]
  .sort_values("mass", ascending=False)
  .assign(bmi=lambda d: d["mass"] / (d["height"] / 100) ** 2))
```

::: {.callout-tip}
## The `.assign` lambda habit
`assign(bmi=lambda d: ...)` names the incoming frame `d` so every expression
inside uses explicit `d["col"]` — no half-updated intermediate state. The
lambda gets called with whatever the chain has produced so far, which is
exactly the pipe's guarantee in R.
:::

## filter ↔ query/mask

```{webr}
#| label: filter-r
library(tidyverse)
genes <- tibble(
  symbol = c("BRCA1", "TP53", "MYC", "GAPDH", "ACTB"),
  chr    = c(17L, 17L, 8L, 12L, 7L),
  log2fc = c(0.4, -1.1, 2.3, 0.0, -0.1),
  padj   = c(0.21, 0.03, 1e-6, 0.98, 0.77)
)

filter(genes, padj < 0.05, abs(log2fc) > 1)   # , means AND
filter(genes, chr %in% c(17, 8))              # membership
filter(genes, is.na(padj) | padj < 0.05)      # NA never passes < — plan for it
```

```{pyodide}
#| label: filter-py
import pandas as pd
genes = pd.DataFrame({
  "symbol": ["BRCA1", "TP53", "MYC", "GAPDH", "ACTB"],
  "chr":    [17, 17, 8, 12, 7],
  "log2fc": [0.4, -1.1, 2.3, 0.0, -0.1],
  "padj":   [0.21, 0.03, 1e-6, 0.98, 0.77]})

print(genes.query("padj < 0.05 and abs(log2fc) > 1"), "\n")
print(genes[genes.chr.isin([17, 8])], "\n")
print(genes[genes.padj.isna() | (genes.padj < 0.05)])
```

::: {.callout-important}
## NaN filter asymmetry — memorize this
`padj < 0.05` is `NA` for missing values in R → those rows **drop silently**.
In pandas the same comparison is `False` → rows also drop. Same outcome, but
R-NA semantics can leak `NA` into downstream `if` statements, while pandas
hides the drop from you. If "how many rows should survive?" matters,
count before and after: `nrow()` / `len()` — the W2D1 audit habit.
:::

## mutate ↔ assign

```{webr}
#| label: mutate-r
genes |>
  mutate(
    sig      = padj < 0.05,
    direction = case_when(
      is.na(padj)                  ~ "unknown",
      padj < 0.05 & log2fc > 0  ~ "up",
      padj < 0.05 & log2fc < 0  ~ "down",
      .default                  = "ns"
    )
  )
```

```{pyodide}
#| label: mutate-py
import numpy as np
genes.assign(
  sig=lambda d: d["padj"] < 0.05,
  direction=lambda d: np.select(
    [d["padj"].isna(),
     (d["padj"] < 0.05) & (d["log2fc"] > 0),
     (d["padj"] < 0.05) & (d["log2fc"] < 0)],
    ["unknown", "up", "down"],
    default="ns"))
```

The translation table for conditional columns:

| R | Python |
|---|---|
| `if_else(cond, yes, no)` | `np.where(cond, yes, no)` |
| `case_when(c1 ~ v1, c2 ~ v2, .default = v3)` | `np.select([c1, c2], [v1, v2], default=v3)` |
| `replace_na(x, 0)` | `s.fillna(0)` |

## The split → apply → combine spine

The single most important wrangling pattern in both languages:

```{webr}
#| label: gsa-r
library(tidyverse)

assay <- tibble(
  treatment = rep(c("control", "treated"), each = 4),
  peptide   = rep(c("SubP", "Vaso"), times = 4),
  conc      = c(10.1, 11.3, 9.8, 12.0, 20.5, 19.2, 21.8, 18.9)
)

assay |>
  group_by(treatment, peptide) |>
  summarise(
    n    = n(),
    mean = mean(conc),
    sd   = sd(conc),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
```

```{pyodide}
#| label: gsa-py
import pandas as pd
assay = pd.DataFrame({
  "treatment": ["control"]*4 + ["treated"]*4,
  "peptide":   ["SubP", "Vaso", "SubP", "Vaso"] * 2,
  "conc":      [10.1, 11.3, 9.8, 12.0, 20.5, 19.2, 21.8, 18.9]})

(assay
  .groupby(["treatment", "peptide"])["conc"]
  .agg(n="count", mean="mean", sd="std")
  .reset_index())
```

Identical output: one row per group, three named summaries. Note the
**`.groups = "drop"`** vs **`.reset_index()`** pairing — both un-nest the
group keys back into plain columns. Skip them and R keeps a grouped df
(mutate acts per-group later!) while pandas gives you a MultiIndex that
breaks naive column access.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Grouped mutate = group-wise z-scores
`group_by(g) |> mutate(z = (x - mean(x)) / sd(x))` computes **within each
group** — the column-window normalization you'll do constantly (batch
correction, per-gene scaling). pandas twin:
`df.groupby("g")["x"].transform(lambda s: (s - s.mean()) / s.std())` —
`transform` keeps the shape, `agg` shrinks it. Shape is the whole difference.
:::

## Row-wise: legal, but the last resort

Sometimes each row genuinely needs its own small computation — per-sample
QC flags over a handful of columns:

```{webr}
#| label: rowwise-r
qc <- tibble(sample = c("S1", "S2", "S3"),
             pct_dup = c(8.1, 22.4, 5.5),
             pct_map = c(91.0, 62.3, 95.2))

qc |>
  rowwise() |>
  mutate(fail = any(pct_dup > 20, pct_map < 80)) |>
  ungroup()
```

```{pyodide}
#| label: rowwise-py
import pandas as pd
qc = pd.DataFrame({"sample": ["S1", "S2", "S3"],
                   "pct_dup": [8.1, 22.4, 5.5],
                   "pct_map": [91.0, 62.3, 95.2]})

qc.assign(fail=(qc["pct_dup"] > 20) | (qc["pct_map"] < 80))
```

The Python answer needed **no** row loop at all — boolean columns combine
column-wise. That's the point of the comparison: R's `rowwise()` is a
deliberate, narrow tool; pandas' `.apply(axis=1)` is the AI-generated smell
that hides vectorizable logic. Rule: **write it column-wise if any way
exists; reach for row-wise only when the operation truly can't broadcast.**

## Drills (live pad)

Predict each output **before** running.

```{webr}
#| label: drills
library(tidyverse)
df <- tibble(g = c("a", "a", "b", "b", "c"),
             x = c(4, 1, 3, 2, 5),
             y = c(10, 20, 30, 40, 50))

# 1. filter(df, g %in% c("a", "c")) — how many rows?

# 2. arrange(df, desc(x)) — first row?

# 3. mutate(df, z = x * y) — z for the g == "c" row?

# 4. count(df, g) — what does the c row say?

# 5. slice_max(df, y, n = 2) — which g's?

# 6. df |> group_by(g) |> summarise(m = mean(x)) — m for b?

# 7. Same but with sd instead of mean — what happens for a group of 1?
#    (add a "d" row with one value to see)

# 8. distinct(df, g) — how many rows?

# 9. pull(df, x) — what type is it? How is it different from df["x"]?

# 10. df |> mutate(rk = min_rank(desc(y))) — rank of the 30?

# 11. filter(df, between(x, 2, 4)) — how many rows?

# 12. df |> group_by(g) |> mutate(n_grp = n()) |> ungroup() — n_grp for a?
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Expected answers
1. 3 rows (a, a, c)
2. g = "c", x = 5
3. 250
4. n = 1
5. c (50) and b (40)
6. 2.5
7. sd of one value is NA — n = 1 groups make sd meaningless; filter `n >= 2` first
8. 3 — one row per unique g (first occurrence wins)
9. A bare numeric vector; `df["x"]` keeps it inside a tibble — `pull` unwraps
10. 4 — min_rank ties share ranks, no gaps (dense_rank has no gaps, row_number never ties)
11. 3 rows (x = 4, 3, 2)
12. 2
:::

## Python drills (live pad)

```{pyodide}
#| label: drills-py
import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame({"g": list("aabbc"),
                   "x": [4, 1, 3, 2, 5],
                   "y": [10, 20, 30, 40, 50]})

# 1. df.query("g in ['a','c']") — how many rows?

# 2. df.sort_values("x", ascending=False).iloc[0] — which g?

# 3. df.assign(z=df.x * df.y).loc[4, "z"]

# 4. df.g.value_counts()["c"]

# 5. df.nlargest(2, "y")["g"].tolist()

# 6. df.groupby("g")["x"].mean()["b"]

# 7. df.groupby("g")["x"].std() — what is it for a 1-row group?

# 8. df.drop_duplicates("g").shape[0]

# 9. df["x"] vs df[["x"]] — which one is a Series, which a DataFrame?

# 10. df["y"].rank(ascending=False) — rank of 30?

# 11. df[df.x.between(2, 4)] — how many rows?

# 12. df.groupby("g")["x"].transform("size") for the first two rows?
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Expected answers (Python)
1. 3
2. c
3. 250
4. 1
5. ['c', 'b']
6. 2.5
7. NaN — same trap as R's `sd` with n = 1
8. 3
9. `df["x"]` = Series; `df[["x"]]` = DataFrame (W1's `[` vs `[[` again!)
10. 4.0 — pandas default rank is average-method; pass `method="min"` for min_rank
11. 3
12. 2 and 2 — `transform` returns a same-length column (vs `agg`'s one-per-group)
:::

## Exercises

### Exercise 1 — top-n per group

Per `peptide`, keep the 2 highest-`conc` observations. R first:

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex-d2-topn
library(tidyverse)
assay <- tibble(
  peptide = rep(c("SubP", "Vaso"), each = 4),
  conc    = c(10.1, 11.3, 25.0, 9.8, 20.5, 19.2, 21.8, 18.9)
)

assay |>
  ______
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex-d2-topn"}
`group_by(peptide) |> slice_max(conc, n = 2)` — verbs compose inside groups.
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex-d2-topn"}
```r
assay |>
  group_by(peptide) |>
  slice_max(conc, n = 2) |>
  ungroup()
```
:::

### Exercise 2 — same, pandas dialect

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: ex-d2-topn-py
import pandas as pd
assay = pd.DataFrame({
  "peptide": ["SubP"]*4 + ["Vaso"]*4,
  "conc":    [10.1, 11.3, 25.0, 9.8, 20.5, 19.2, 21.8, 18.9]})

______
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex-d2-topn-py"}
`groupby("peptide", group_keys=False).apply(lambda d: d.nlargest(2, "conc"))`
— or the slicker sort-then-head trick.
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex-d2-topn-py"}
```python
(assay
  .sort_values("conc", ascending=False)
  .groupby("peptide")
  .head(2))
# sort once globally, then head(2) per group — avoids the .apply entirely
```
:::

### Exercise 3 — conditional column, three-way

Add `direction`: "up" if `log2fc > 1` and `padj < 0.05`; "down" if
`log2fc < -1` and `padj < 0.05`; else "ns". R first, then Python.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex-d2-direction
library(tidyverse)
de <- tibble(
  gene   = c("A", "B", "C", "D"),
  log2fc = c(2.1, -1.8, 0.5, 3.0),
  padj   = c(0.01, 0.02, 0.01, 0.40)
)

de |>
  ______
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex-d2-direction"}
`case_when()` — order matters; the first TRUE wins.
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex-d2-direction"}
```r
de |>
  mutate(direction = case_when(
    padj < 0.05 & log2fc >  1 ~ "up",
    padj < 0.05 & log2fc < -1 ~ "down",
    .default = "ns"
  ))
```
:::

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: ex-d2-direction-py
import pandas as pd
de = pd.DataFrame({
  "gene":   list("ABCD"),
  "log2fc": [2.1, -1.8, 0.5, 3.0],
  "padj":   [0.01, 0.02, 0.01, 0.40]})

______
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex-d2-direction-py"}
`np.select([cond1, cond2], ["up", "down"], default="ns")` — first-listed wins,
same as case_when.
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex-d2-direction-py"}
```python
import numpy as np
de.assign(direction=np.select(
  [(de.padj < 0.05) & (de.log2fc >  1),
   (de.padj < 0.05) & (de.log2fc < -1)],
  ["up", "down"], default="ns"))
```
:::

### Exercise 4 — group-wise normalization

Within each `batch`, express every `conc` as a z-score. This is the column
you'd use before comparing batches. Both dialects.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex-d2-zscore
library(tidyverse)
dat <- tibble(
  batch = c("B1", "B1", "B2", "B2", "B2"),
  conc  = c(10, 12, 20, 24, 22)
)

dat |>
  ______
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex-d2-zscore"}
grouped `mutate`: `(conc - mean(conc)) / sd(conc)`.
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex-d2-zscore"}
```r
dat |>
  group_by(batch) |>
  mutate(z = (conc - mean(conc)) / sd(conc)) |>
  ungroup()
```
:::

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: ex-d2-zscore-py
import pandas as pd
dat = pd.DataFrame({"batch": ["B1","B1","B2","B2","B2"],
                    "conc":  [10, 12, 20, 24, 22]})

______
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex-d2-zscore-py"}
`groupby("batch")["conc"].transform(...)` — transform keeps row alignment.
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex-d2-zscore-py"}
```python
dat.assign(z=dat.groupby("batch")["conc"]
             .transform(lambda s: (s - s.mean()) / s.std()))
```
:::

### Exercise 5 — the AI-code refactor

Refactor the loop below into verbs. It computes, per sample, whether ANY
metric failed QC. R version:

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex-d2-refactor
qc <- data.frame(
  sample  = c("S1", "S2", "S3"),
  pct_dup = c(8.1, 22.4, 5.5),
  reads_m = c(21.0, 4.2, 18.9)
)

# ❌ AI-smell: loop + growing vector (W1's forbidden pattern, with a for-loop)
out <- c()
for (i in 1:nrow(qc)) {
  out[i] <- qc$pct_dup[i] > 20 || qc$reads_m[i] < 10
}
qc$fail <- out

# ✅ Your turn — vectorized dplyr, no loop, no c()
______
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex-d2-refactor"}
Two boolean columns OR'd together: `mutate(fail = pct_dup > 20 | reads_m < 10)`.
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex-d2-refactor"}
```r
qc |> mutate(fail = pct_dup > 20 | reads_m < 10)
# recognize-the-smell: `||` is scalar-only (and now errors on vectors —
# the loop used `||` on length-1 slices so it "worked"); row loops that
# could be column ops are the #1 AI-R tell.
```
:::

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: ex-d2-refactor-py
import pandas as pd
qc = pd.DataFrame({"sample":  ["S1", "S2", "S3"],
                   "pct_dup": [8.1, 22.4, 5.5],
                   "reads_m": [21.0, 4.2, 18.9]})

# ❌ AI-smell: df.apply(axis=1) with a per-row if/else
qc["fail"] = qc.apply(lambda r: r["pct_dup"] > 20 or r["reads_m"] < 10, axis=1)

# ✅ Your turn — column-wise, no apply
______
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex-d2-refactor-py"}
`(qc["pct_dup"] > 20) | (qc["reads_m"] < 10)` — pandas needs explicit
parentheses; `|` binds tighter than comparison!
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex-d2-refactor-py"}
```python
qc["fail"] = (qc["pct_dup"] > 20) | (qc["reads_m"] < 10)
# recognize-the-smell: apply(axis=1) runs a Python function per row —
# 100x slower on big frames and, worse, it hides vectorizable logic.
```
:::

## Common pitfalls (real ones)

::: {.callout-warning}
## 1. Grouped state leaks
In R, a `group_by` you never `ungroup()` makes every later `mutate` per-group
— silent wrongness three steps later. In pandas, forgetting `reset_index()`
after `agg` leaves a MultiIndex that breaks `df["col"]`. **End every
grouped pipeline with the un-nesting step** (or a comment saying why not).
:::

::: {.callout-warning}
## 2. pandas `|` without parentheses
`df.a > 1 | df.b < 2` parses as `df.a > (1 | df.b) < 2` — bitwise `|`
binds **tighter** than comparisons in Python (opposite of R, where `|`
sits between `and` and the comparisons). Each side needs explicit
parentheses.
:::

::: {.callout-warning}
## 3. Chained assignment vanishes
`df[df.g == "a"]["x"] = 0` — the classic SettingWithCopyWarning: you edited
a copy; the original is untouched (or a view was — undefined!). One `.loc`
call does it right: `df.loc[df.g == "a", "x"] = 0`. The dplyr twin `filter()
|> mutate()` is safe because verbs always return fresh frames — one of the
few places R is *less* trap-prone.
:::

::: {.callout-warning}
## 4. `summarise` on an empty group
After a filter that removes everything, `summarise(mean(x))` returns `NA`/NaN
in R, errors or NaN in pandas depending on the agg — never a helpful
message. Guard: check `nrow()`/`len()` before summarising filtered data.
:::

## Self-quiz — predict the output

```{webr}
#| label: quiz
library(tidyverse)
df <- tibble(g = c("a", "a", "b"), x = c(1, 2, 3), y = c(9, 9, 9))

# Q1
df |> filter(x > 1) |> nrow()

# Q2
df |> group_by(g) |> summarise(m = mean(x)) |> nrow()

# Q3
df |> mutate(z = x > 1) |> pull(z) |> typeof()

# Q4
df |> arrange(g, desc(x)) |> slice(1) |> pull(x)

# Q5
df |> group_by(g) |> mutate(n = n()) |> filter(n == 2) |> nrow()
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Quiz answers
1. 2
2. 2 — one row per group
3. "logical" — comparisons make logical columns, not 0/1 numerics
4. 2 — group a first (arrange on g), and within a the larger x
5. 2 — only group a has n == 2; both of its rows survive
:::

## Wrap-up checklist

- [ ] The 6 verbs and their pandas method-twins — no notes needed
- [ ] `group_by + summarise` ↔ `groupby + agg` with un-nesting at the end
- [ ] Grouped `mutate` ↔ `transform` — shape stays, group means computed within
- [ ] `case_when` ↔ `np.select`, first condition wins in both
- [ ] Row-wise ops are the last resort in both languages
